Intuition certainly has value; experts develop a swift, wordless sense of judgement built from years of experience. paragraph_raw: You've become known for changing your mind in public, which most leaders avoid. Doesn't it make you look inconsistent? paragraph_raw: Under certain conditions, hot water appears to freeze faster than cold water, a puzzle known as the Mpemba effect. His teacher dismissed the observation, but Mpemba later published it with a physics professor. paragraph_raw: Why do we remember the first and last items on a list better than those in the middle? Psychologists call this the serial position effect. The last items are still fresh in short-term memory when we are asked to recall them. Items in the middle get neither advantage. The effect has consequences. paragraph_raw: The intuition that seeing is believing, that visual perception offers a direct and faithful window onto reality, is among the most deeply rooted and least examined of human convictions. Neuroscience has steadily dismantled it. What we experience as effortless, immediate sight is in fact an elaborate construction, in which the brain interprets fragmentary and ambiguous signals through the lens of expectation and prior experience, actively generating a coherent scene rather than passively receiving one. We do not see the world; we see the brain's best hypothesis about the world, mistaken, almost irresistibly, for the world itself.

paragraph_raw: It is often supposed that the opposite of a courageous life is a cowardly one, and that the chief obstacle to living well is therefore the failure of nerve in the face of obvious dangers. paragraph_raw: In 1975, the British economist Charles Goodhart observed that statistical relationships tend to collapse once policymakers try to use them for control. The idea, later summarised as Goodhart's law, holds that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Hospitals judged on waiting times may find ways to shorten the official queue rather than treat patients faster; schools assessed by exam results may teach narrowly to the test. In each case, people do not act dishonestly; they simply respond rationally to the incentive in front of them. The implication is uncomfortable for anyone designing performance indicators: the very act of rewarding a number can corrupt the information it was meant to provide, which is why institutions rely on several measures and on human judgement rather than on any single figure.

paragraph_raw: For fifteen years, Ozan had earned his living translating novels, and he had always assumed that his craft was safe from machines, since literature depended on nuance. paragraph_raw: During the Second World War, the American military examined bombers returning from missions and noted where they had been hit by enemy fire, planning to add armour where damage was heaviest. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out a flaw in this reasoning. The planes being studied were the ones that had survived; the holes showed where an aircraft could be hit and still return. The areas with no damage on the surviving planes, such as the engines, were probably where hits had been fatal, since those planes never came back to be counted. Armour, he argued, belonged where the returning planes were unmarked. This error, now called survivorship bias, appears whenever we draw conclusions only from successes, as when people study famous entrepreneurs who left university and conclude that dropping out leads to wealth.

paragraph_raw: Few inventions are as omnipresent as the humble shipping container. Before the 1950s, cargo was loaded piece by piece, in sacks, barrels and crates, by large teams of dock workers; a ship could spend longer in port than at sea, and theft was common. In 1956, the American trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean sent the first container ship from New Jersey to Texas, carrying standard metal boxes that could be lifted directly from lorries onto the ship. Loading costs fell dramatically. Within a few decades, standard container sizes had been agreed internationally, ports had been redesigned around enormous cranes, and global trade had expanded in ways that would have been unthinkable before. The change also had a human cost: traditional dock work, and the close-knit communities built around it, largely disappeared.

paragraph_raw: The term 'placebo effect' is familiar, but its lesser-known counterpart, the nocebo effect, may be as important. When patients expect a treatment to cause harm, they are more likely to experience side effects, even if the treatment is inactive. In clinical trials, a substantial proportion of participants given sugar pills report headaches, nausea or fatigue, often matching the side effects listed on the consent form. Researchers believe that anxiety and expectation alter how the brain interprets bodily sensations, turning ordinary aches into perceived symptoms. This creates a dilemma for doctors. They are ethically obliged to inform patients about possible risks, yet the way that information is delivered may make those risks more likely. Some studies suggest that framing, such as emphasising how many patients tolerate a drug well, can reduce the effect without withholding information.

paragraph_raw: In 2022, sixty-one British companies took part in a six-month trial of a four-day working week, in which employees kept their full pay while working around twenty per cent fewer hours. The results surprised many sceptics. Revenue at participating firms stayed broadly the same, while staff reported less stress and burnout and took fewer sick days. By the end, fifty-six of the companies had decided to continue with the shorter week, at least for now. Critics, however, point out that the firms volunteered to take part and were therefore likely to be well suited to the change, and that the model may be far harder to apply in hospitals, schools or factories, where work cannot simply be squeezed into fewer days.

paragraph_raw: Many astronauts describe a powerful change in outlook after seeing the Earth from space, an experience the writer Frank White named the overview effect in 1987. From orbit, the planet appears as a small, fragile ball suspended in darkness, its atmosphere a thin blue line, and national borders, so important on the ground, are invisible. Some astronauts have returned with a strong sense of connection to humanity and concern for the environment. Others describe something closer to grief: the actor William Shatner, after a brief flight in 2021, said he felt overwhelming sadness at the contrast between the cold emptiness of space and the warmth of life below. Researchers are now testing whether virtual reality can produce a similar shift in ordinary people.

paragraph_raw: Newspaper headlines are often written in a compressed style that drops small words such as articles and verbs, and this can produce sentences that are unintentionally ambiguous. A classic example is 'Squad helps dog bite victim', which could mean that a team assisted someone who had been bitten or, absurdly, that it helped a dog to bite someone. Linguists collect such 'crash blossoms', named after a headline that read 'Violinist linked to JAL crash blossoms', which puzzled readers until they realised it referred to a violinist, connected to a plane crash, whose career was blossoming. These amusing errors reveal how much our understanding depends on context and on the tiny grammatical words we usually overlook.

paragraph_raw: For twenty years, Nesrin had told herself that she would learn to play the piano once life became less busy. There was always a reason to wait: exams, then a demanding job, then two children who filled every evening. On her forty-fifth birthday, her daughter handed her an envelope containing a voucher for ten lessons. Nesrin's first reaction was embarrassment; she imagined a teacher sighing at her clumsy fingers alongside gifted eight-year-olds. Yet the teacher, an elderly man with a patient smile, told her that adults often progress faster at first, because they practise deliberately and understand what they are aiming for. Six months later, Nesrin played a Chopin waltz at a concert, her hands trembling but steady enough. Afterwards, her daughter whispered, 'You see? There was never going to be a less busy time.'

paragraph_raw: I read that our city is planning to ban cars from the old town centre on weekends. Good. The streets are so narrow that walking there is miserable. I see your point, but think about the shopkeepers. Many of their customers drive in from the suburbs. Some cities found the opposite, though. When streets became pedestrian-only, people stayed longer and spent more. Perhaps, but that depends on good public transport, and ours is unreliable. The buses on my route come every forty minutes, if they come at all. So the ban should come with better buses, not instead of them. Exactly. If they do both, I'd support it. If they only do the ban, I suspect it will just move the traffic jams to the surrounding streets.

paragraph_raw: A five-year study involving dozens of primary schools has found that pupils who spend at least one lesson a week learning outdoors, in school gardens or nearby parks, show measurable improvements in concentration and attendance. Researchers compared schools that adopted the programme with similar schools that did not, and found that absences fell by around eight per cent in participating classes. Teachers reported fewer behaviour problems, particularly among pupils who usually struggled to sit still. The authors are careful to note that the schools volunteered for the programme, which means their teachers may have been unusually motivated, and they call for a larger randomised trial before the approach is adopted more widely.
